planting.note: Scarify seed and fall-sow with cold stratification into a fast-draining high-elevation rock garden or gravel bed; currently scarce in commercial trade, so expect to source seed from a specialty supplier.

directions: A genuine high-elevation rock-garden curiosity, this milkvetch is prized for its large, inflated, red-mottled balloon-like seedpods, a distinctive feature rather than merely a rangeland curiosity. It supports an exceptional range of native bees, butterflies, and moths as both a nectar source and caterpillar host. Native to alpine fellfield through subalpine and yellow pine forest from 2,500 to 12,000 feet, it needs sharp drainage and minimal summer water once established.

planting.note: Scarify and sand or hot-water soak seed, then sow with cold stratification into a rock garden with perfect drainage; in wetter parts of California, site under a rock overhang to stay dry.

directions: Widely regarded as the handsomest milkvetch of the desert, this species carries genuinely unusual bright scarlet pea-flowers, unlike the purple, white, or cream flowers typical of the genus, and attracts hummingbirds along with several butterfly larvae including Painted Lady and Melissa Blue. Its gray-woolly foliage forms an attractive, compact clump about a foot across — a true rock-garden specimen that loves the heat. Give it just enough water to establish, then reduce significantly, since perfect drainage is essential.

planting.note: Soak seed in hot water 24 hours and sow fresh in fall into sandy, loamy, clay, or high-calcium-carbonate soil; not currently known to be commercially cultivated, so source seed from a specialty supplier.

directions: A highly adaptable milkvetch tolerant of sand, loam, clay, and high-calcium-carbonate soils, this species carries distinctive mottled, red-and-cream freckled seedpods and supports an exceptional range of native bees, butterflies, and moths. It is also the species most prominently studied in livestock locoweed-poisoning research due to swainsonine content, so site it away from grazing animals and pastured livestock. It is drought-tolerant once established and useful for difficult dry sites where few other legumes perform.

planting.note: Soak seed 24 hours in water and sow in fall; germination is slow and uneven over up to four months. Plant on a coastal bluff, dune, or rocky outcrop with salt and wind exposure.

directions: A California coastal bluff and dune native forming thick, tangled, sprawling clumps usable as a salt-tolerant, deer-resistant ground cover, this milkvetch blooms nearly year-round with cream to pale-purple-tinted flowers and supports strong pollinator and butterfly-moth caterpillar relationships. Pair it with sand verbena, saltbush, and beach evening primrose for a seaside xeriscape planting. Germination is notably slow and erratic, so be patient and consider starting several seed lots at once.
